finalText:
**Merge** creates a new commit that connects two branches. Both branch histories stay in the log, so you can see that they existed separately and came together.

**Rebase** replays one branch's commits on top of the other, rewriting their history so the result looks like one straight line. The old commits are gone from the log.

**Use merge** when you want to keep the record of where changes came from — typically when someone else's work is joining yours, or when a feature branch is coming back to main. It's the safe default for shared branches.

**Use rebase** when you're cleaning up your own commits before sharing them, or pulling the latest main into your local feature branch so you don't fall behind. It keeps history tidy and linear. Never rebase commits that have already been pushed to a branch other people are working on — it rewrites history they're depending on, and creates a mess.

The mental model: merge says "these two lines of work happened and joined"; rebase says "I'm reorganizing my work so it looks like it was always built on top of the latest version."
